meta: Fernando Gallego's Pietà, about 1490 to 1500: the Virgin mourns her dead son in front of the cross, with a Gothic town behind.
about: Pebbles, a bone and a skull lie on the ground around the Virgin Mary as she looks down at her dead son across her lap. Behind the cross, a walled Gothic town sits between water and green countryside. Fernando Gallego took his cue from Northern European painting. The Getty adds that he kept to Spanish habits, with a subdued palette and unidealized figures. Where Netherlandish painters dwelt on fine detail in nature, he cut away whatever distracted from grief. The cross carries the letters INRI.

meta: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo's 1743 oval sketch of angels carrying the Holy House to Loreto, a study for a lost Venetian ceiling fresco.
about: Angels carry a small house through the clouds in this oval sketch, with the Virgin and Child seated on top. Giovanni Battista Tiepolo painted it in 1743 as the last preparatory study for a ceiling fresco in the Scalzi church in Venice. Bombing in World War I destroyed the fresco. The subject is a legend that the Virgin's house in Nazareth flew from the Holy Land to Loreto. Tiepolo made the lowest figures large and the upper ones small, so the ceiling seems to open upward.

meta: Hans Holbein the Younger's drawing of an unknown scholar or cleric in a round cap, made in chalk, ink and brush about 1532 to 1535.
about: A man in a round cap and loose gown is drawn in profile, and nobody knows who he was. Hans Holbein the Younger began with black chalk, then used brush and ink for the hair and collar. A pointed quill drew the contours and the small dots of stubble. Red chalk over the pink ground modelled the face. Holbein became painter to Henry VIII in 1536. Many court drawings were found in his studio after his death in 1543, and the Getty says this sheet may have been among them.

meta: Domenico Fetti's Portrait of a Man with a Sheet of Music, about 1620: a bearded man points at an upturned bowl, a vanitas symbol.
about: A bearded man in theatrical clothes points at an upturned bowl while holding a sheet of music. The bowl is a vanitas symbol, a reminder that material things are empty. Two young men in the lower right corner watch him with interest. Domenico Fetti painted it about 1620. The Getty suggests the sitter may have been a singer or an actor in a role from a play, and that his informal manner could mean he was a friend of the artist. His eyes meet the viewer.

meta: Frans Snijders's Larder Still Life with Housekeeper and Young Boy, 1636 to 1638: a boy grabs grapes in a crowded pantry.
about: A boy sitting on a larder table reaches for a fistful of grapes while the housekeeper puts a hand on his shoulder to scold him. The table is crowded with baskets and platters of apples, peaches and pomegranates, and dead fowl wait to be prepared. In the window at upper right, a cat provokes two dogs below. Frans Snijders painted this pantry scene between 1636 and 1638. It is in the Getty Museum.

meta: Polidoro da Caravaggio's red chalk study of a naked man with raised arms, about 1535, probably made for a martyrdom scene.
about: A naked man with raised arms lets his head droop, drawn in red chalk with strong diagonal shading on the chest, arms and thighs. Polidoro da Caravaggio put his effort into the body and left the head loose. Along the top of the sheet is a second sketch of a pointed foot and calf. The Getty links the study to a martyrdom scene. When the museum bought the sheet, the arm at the right edge was attached wrongly along the bottom. Conservators moved it back.

meta: Bronzino's Portrait of Ugolino Martelli, about 1540: a Florentine scholar with Homer and Bembo, in front of his family palazzo.
about: Ugolino Martelli, a young Florentine scholar, rests his arm on a work by Pietro Bembo while a Greek copy of Homer's Iliad lies open beside him at the start of book nine. Bronzino signed the table edge BRONZO FIORENTINO. Behind the sitter stands the family palazzo, along with a marble David once credited to Donatello and now given to Antonio or Bernardo Rossellino. David stood for Florentine freedom, so he may allude to Martelli's republican politics. A second book is marked MARO, for Virgil.

meta: Pompeo Batoni's 1769 double portrait of Emperor Joseph II and his brother Leopold, Grand Duke of Tuscany.
about: Two brothers in court dress stand side by side: Joseph II, Holy Roman Emperor, and Leopold, then Grand Duke of Tuscany. Pompeo Batoni painted them in 1769. He was a Rome portraitist who made his name painting British visitors on the Grand Tour. Leopold would later succeed his brother as emperor, in 1790. Wikipedia calls the double portrait one of the more famous images of its era. It hangs in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna.

meta: Andrea Mantegna's Pallas Expelling the Vices from the Garden of Virtue, painted for Isabella d'Este's studiolo about 1499.
about: A helmeted Minerva with a spear drives the Vices out of a walled garden. Andrea Mantegna painted it for the studiolo of Isabella d'Este, as the second picture he made for that room after the Parnassus. The Vices are ugly figures labelled with scrolls in a medieval manner. Idleness is chased, and Minerva also rescues Diana from a centaur. Beside her stands a tree with human features. High in the sky hover Justice, Temperance and Fortitude.

meta: Pietro Perugino's Madonna and Child with Saints John the Baptist and Catherine of Alexandria, about 1495, in the Louvre.
about: One cartoon served for three Madonna panels by Pietro Perugino, with very little change between them. The others are in Vienna and in the Städel Museum. This version, from about 1495, adds John the Baptist and Catherine of Alexandria, who holds a palm frond and a spiked wheel. Wikipedia reports that the Madonna's face is based on Chiara Fancelli, the painter's wife. Gold halos rise above all three figures. The panel is in the Louvre.

meta: Pietro Perugino's round panel of the Madonna and Child with two angels and Saints Rose and Catherine, now in the Louvre.
about: A round panel seats the Virgin on a blue-draped throne with the Christ Child, two angels above and Saints Rose and Catherine on either side. One saint holds a rose branch, the other a palm and a book. Wikipedia dates the work to about 1490 and gives it to Pietro Perugino together with Andrea Aloigi. It was sold from the collection of William II of the Netherlands in 1850. It went to the Louvre, where it is on display.

meta: Ambrosius Benson's The Concert after the Meal, about 1540: a music party at a table, later owned by Hermann Göring and recovered after the war.
about: Around a dining table with fruit, sheet music and a lute, richly dressed men and women play instruments, while arches open onto a river and a castle. Ambrosius Benson's painting passed through the dealer Paul Graupe and then to Hermann Göring, who according to the scholar Marlier bought it for the planned museum at Linz. After the war it was recovered from the Central Collecting Point in Munich and assigned to the Louvre. Later it was lent to the château at Blois.

meta: Frans Hals's 1620 portrait of Catharina Both van der Eem, the pendant to his portrait of Paulus van Beresteyn.
about: Catharina Both van der Eem stands beside a carved chair with one hand on its arm, in a black dress with a gold-embroidered bodice and a wide lace collar. Frans Hals painted her in 1620 as a pendant to his portrait of Paulus van Beresteyn. Wikipedia treats the two as a pair, and both are in the Louvre.

meta: A pen and ink anatomical study of a kneeling man, catalogued as by a follower of Michelangelo and once owned by Jacques-Louis David.
about: A kneeling man seen from the side is drawn in pen and brown ink, with hatching for the muscles of his back, thigh and legs. Below is a separate study of tendons and muscle fibres. The sheet is catalogued as by a follower of Michelangelo, but it was sold in London in 1915 as a work by Michelangelo himself. Inscriptions on it name Charles I of England and the painter Jacques-Louis David as earlier owners. The Chicago collector William Gurley bought it at that sale. It was given to the Art Institute in 1922.
credit_line: The Leonora Hall Gurley Memorial Collection

meta: J. M. W. Turner's watercolour of Mussooree and the Dhoon seen from Landour, about 1835, now at the Art Institute of Chicago.
about: A hazy valley opens beneath layered blue mountains, with a road winding through the hills and travellers resting beside a loaded pony in the foreground. J. M. W. Turner made the watercolour about 1835. It later belonged to the Royal Artillery Institution at Woolwich, which sold it at Sotheby's in London in 1960. Dealers handled it next, and Dorothy Braude Edinburg of Brookline bought it. She gave it to the Art Institute of Chicago in 2013.
credit_line: Gift of Dorothy Braude Edinburg to the Harry B. and Bessie K. Braude Memorial Collection

meta: Jan van Eyck's small diptych of the Crucifixion and the Last Judgment, about 1420, probably made for private devotion.
about: Two small panels show the Crucifixion on one side and the Last Judgment on the other. Jan van Eyck is credited with them, though unidentified followers or workshop members finished parts. A Wikipedia account says the pair was probably commissioned for private devotion. On the left, mourners crowd the foreground beneath a view of Jerusalem. On the right, a hell scene sits at the base and Christ in Majesty at the top. Inscriptions appear in Greek, Latin and Hebrew. The frames carry Latin Bible passages.
